# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

# edfringe-allocator — this project's own rules

The working knowledge of the EdFringe Allocator pipeline: what may touch the network,
what a year folder owes the solver, and the one datetime invariant everything downstream
assumes. Three of these are checks (`edfringe/offline-stage-imports`,
`edfringe/year-folder-contract`, `edfringe/no-credentialed-path`).

## Datetimes are naive Europe/London, everywhere

Every datetime in the data model is a **naive ISO string in Europe/London local time**
(`edfringe/model.py:3`). Conversion happens once, at the fetch boundary:
`edfringe/extract.py` parses the UTC timestamps out of the fetched event and does
`dt.astimezone(LONDON).replace(tzinfo=None)` (`edfringe/extract.py:78-79`). Downstream —
the solver, the verifier, the renderer, the calendar image — compares those strings and
`datetime.fromisoformat` values directly.

So: never let an aware datetime past `extract`. Mixing one in raises `TypeError` on the
first comparison, usually deep inside the solver where the cause is unrecognisable.
`edfringe/planner_ics.py` is the one place timezone names appear again, and only as iCal
`TZID=Europe/London` text on the way out.

## Code is year-agnostic; only `years/<YYYY>/` changes

Starting a new Fringe year is a **new data folder, never a code edit** — see
`years/README.md` and the `start-a-new-fringe-year` skill in this pack. The window and
the travel buffers reach the solver through `cli.py:73-80` →
`edfringe.scheduling.configure()`, so `years/<YYYY>/config.json` is the source of truth.

Known drift to fix rather than copy: `edfringe/scheduling.py:14-18` still carries the
2026 window and gap values as module defaults, and `edfringe/render.py:139` hardcodes
"Edinburgh Fringe 2026" in the schedule heading. Both are overridden or cosmetic today;
neither is a pattern to follow when adding code.

## The favourites input is a CSV export, not scraped HTML

A view-source of the edfringe.com favourites page is the **logged-out empty state** — it
does not contain the favourites (`docs/FINDINGS.md` §2, README "Good to know" #1). The
resolved design reads the URL column out of the user's CSV export
(`years/<YYYY>/favorites.csv` → `edfringe/favorites.py`). Do not re-attempt to fetch or
parse the favourites page; it is a dead end that has already been paid for once.

## Never introduce a credentialed path

Enforced by `edfringe/no-credentialed-path`; what stays here is why the answer is never
"add the credential". An earlier `cookies.json` held live `auth_token`/`access_token`
for `.edfringe.com` and was committed (`docs/FINDINGS.md` §5) — and it bought nothing,
because show pages are public. The two steps that genuinely need a login (exporting the
favourites CSV, and buying tickets) run in the owner's own browser
(`docs/CLAUDE_FOR_BROWSER.md`), so a change that wants a login is a change that has
taken a wrong turn: move that step to the browser rather than hand the repo a secret.
The retired `old/` prototype still carries the playwright cookie-jar login it was
replaced for — kept for reference, never a pattern to copy.

## `shows_raw/` is the durable source; re-fetching is opt-in

`years/<YYYY>/shows_raw/<slug>.json` is committed and is the source everything else
re-derives from (`edfringe/extract.py` reads it offline). A normal run of the `Fetch show
data` Action re-downloads **nothing** — only the `refresh` input pulls fresh availability
(`.github/workflows/fetch.yml`). Fetching is the one networked stage, so it runs in CI;
extract / travel / schedule / verify / image all run offline from what is committed.

# Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing)

Each pack states what it owns and what it does not. When a rule, doc, skill or check could live in more than one, this table decides it — and "no pack fits" means a new pack or the project's own `local_packs/`, never the baseline by default.

| Pack | Belongs | Does not belong |
|---|---|---|
| `barriers` | directed folder-access graph rules — which directories may never reference which, plus the exceptions each rule allows | where a file should live or naming conventions — that is basics file-placement, not an access barrier |
| `basics` | cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills | technology-specific content — its own tech pack; GitHub Actions workflow or platform behaviour — github-actions; git procedure — git-github |
| `git-github` | git and GitHub procedure: commit layering, branch and merge mechanics, squash-merge recovery, PR and merge-to-main commands | the issue-branch-PR lifecycle rules themselves — basics; workflow YAML and Actions runtime behaviour — github-actions |
| `github-actions` | workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls | git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack |
| `grow_with_claudinite` | rules and tasks for capturing lessons into local packs — extraction, dedup, conversation logs, skill-usage folding | repo housekeeping of issues, PRs and branches — that is tidy-repo; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `tidy-repo` | housekeeping of open issues, pull requests and branches in one repo — triage verdicts, standing trackers, assess-vs-act policy | extracting lessons into packs — that is grow_with_claudinite; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `edfringe-allocator` (local) | the allocator pipeline — its offline/network stage split, per-year data contract, naive-Europe/London datetime invariant | portable practice and general repo hygiene — those live in the vendored Claudinite canon |

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

The deterministic self-refresh already ran. Before you were dispatched, this task's
**preprocessing** (`worker.mjs`, a code subprocess) converged this repo's
`.claudinite/shared/` mount to the current canon head, converged the wiring, applied
the **mechanical** migration notes, and pushed the result as one commit on the
per-cycle **maintenance PR**. You are here only because it left **residual work you alone can do** —
a pending *agentic* migration note, a workflow file its token was not permitted to push
(§2b), and/or a conformance finding the deterministic auto-fix could not resolve. **Do not re-run the mechanical
converge** (it is done, in the repo); your job is the judgment remainder, on that
same PR.

You run under the executor, GitHub writes go through the session's **MCP tools**
(`mcp__github__*`), and — unlike before — the Claudinite canon is **not** in your
session (agent-preprocessing DESIGN §7/E5). Everything you need is in THIS repo: the
migration notes are in your own vendored mount
(`.claudinite/shared/migrations/active_migrations/`), and the maintenance branch is
already open. The dispatch issue's **Context** is binding scope — do not widen it.

## 1. Continue on the open maintenance PR

**The dispatch issue names what preprocessing created**, under `### Delivered by
preprocessing` — a PR number and a branch ref. That section is your source for them.

- **A PR marked `(open)`** — make every change below on its head branch. Never the
  default branch, never a new branch.
- **A PR marked `(already merged)`** — normal on a repo with no `pull_request` CI, where
  preprocessing merges in the same run. Its content has landed; further work goes on a
  fresh PR of your own (§2b says where).
- **No `### Delivered` section** — preprocessing created nothing this cycle. §2 and §3
  may still have work; only when §2, §2b and §3 all come up empty is this run a no-op to
  comment and close.

## 2. Apply the pending flagged-agentic migration note(s)

Read this repo's stamp (`.claudinite-checks.json` → `claudinite.updated`): preprocessing
**held** it at the day before the earliest pending agentic note. Every
`.claudinite/shared/migrations/active_migrations/` record whose `landed` date is **on or
after** that day (same-day inclusive, #330) and which carries an `agentic: { model,
instructions }` note is yours to apply, **oldest first**. Follow each note's own
`instructions` exactly — they describe member-side adaptation no script can do (e.g.
adapting this repo's `.claudinite/local/packs/` content to a changed engine contract).
A note that finds nothing to adapt in THIS repo is a no-op — that is normal and
correct; never invent a change to justify the run.

## 2b. Land the workflow files preprocessing could not push

Preprocessing pushes with the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which GitHub never permits to
create or update a file under `.github/workflows/` — and because the refusal rejects the
whole ref, the converge **withholds** those paths from its commit rather than losing the
entire push to them. Your MCP writes go through a credential that *does* hold the
`workflows` permission, so landing them is yours, and only yours: nothing else in the
cycle can.

Rediscover the list the same way preprocessing produced it — this part is deterministic,
not a search: in a checkout of the branch §1 named (or the default branch when its PR
already merged), run `node .claudinite/shared/migrations/apply.mjs` (the mechanical
apply, idempotent) and compare `.github/workflows/` against what it wrote. The head
commit's message also names each withheld path, as a cross-check.

Commit whatever differs, via the MCP tools, and **where it goes depends on what §1's
`### Delivered` section said**:

- **The PR is `(open)`** — commit to its head branch, so the cycle stays one reviewable
  change.
- **The PR is `(already merged)`, or no section at all** — open your own PR against the
  default branch carrying only these files, and deliver it per this repo's
  `maintenance.delivery` exactly as §4 describes. This is within the task's `merged-pr`
  ceiling. **Comment its number on this dispatch issue**, so the next run finds it by
  association rather than by guessing at its name.

Either way the file must land this cycle. It is not deferrable: preprocessing withholds it
on *every* run, so leaving it produces a repo that reports a clean converge forever while
the file never arrives.

A cycle that withheld nothing leaves nothing to do here, which is the ordinary case: the
files are byte-identical to their templates and the apply writes nothing at all. Never
hand-edit these copies to match something else — the template is canon, and the next cycle
re-materializes it.

I dug into issue #82, the workflow run behind it, and the code that dispatched it. Read-only investigation — no changes made.

## What actually happened

**The run:** scheduler run [31092180798](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator/actions/runs/31092180798), event `workflow_dispatch`, actor `missingbulb`, `CLAUDINITE_OVERRIDES: FORCE_TASKS=baselining`, at 10:10:34 — 7 minutes after the 10:03 scheduled run. So the *dispatch* was a deliberate manual force. `FORCE_TASKS` skips the precondition entirely (`run.mjs:42,198` → `FORCED_VERDICT`), which is why the issue body carries that "nothing here asserts there is work to do" Context.

**But the force did not cause the agent.** Forcing only guarantees the *worker* runs. The agent stage is gated separately: `run.mjs:624` files `ready-for-agent` **iff** the worker writes `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`. The log line is `preprocessing basics/baselining [d2026-08-06]: ok (agent requested)` — the worker asked for it.

**What the worker did:** a real converge. It delivered PR #81 → `64df550`, 11 files, +493/−70 — new scheduler `preprocess.mjs`/`run.mjs`/`dispatch.mjs`, the workflow-withholding registry guard, the `2026-08-05-sheepdog-fleet-baseline` record. The 03:45 scheduled run had missed all of it because canon moved afterwards. That half of the run earned its keep.

**Why it escalated to an agent — not recoverable from the log, and here's why that matters.** The gate at the time (`shouldRequestAgent`, pre-#81) had three branches:
- *pending agentic note* — ruled out: the delivered stamp is `2026-08-06T10:10:44Z`, i.e. **not held back**, which the worker only does when a note is pending. The only `agentic` record (`2026-07-19-pack-independence`) predates the prior stamp (`2026-08-05`).
- *withheld workflow file* — didn't exist yet; `withheldCount` landed in the very commit this run delivered.
- *`meaningfulChange && !checksPass`, or a failed self-test* — by elimination, this fired.

I can't reproduce it: on the exact tree that was committed (`64df550`), `check_the_world.mjs` exits 0 with 33 rules and `selftest.mjs --strict` passes — both in a working dir and in a `--depth=1` shallow clone matching the runner's checkout. And the Actions log has no worker output at all, because pre-#81 `runPreprocessing` buffered the child's stdout and discarded it on success. The live-echo fix is *in #81* — delivered by this very run, so the next occurrence will be diagnosable and this one never will be.

**One more artifact of the same skew:** the issue has no `### Delivered by preprocessing` section even though preprocessing delivered and merged #81. The run executed the *old* `dispatch.mjs` (that section is #81's addition), while the agent read the *new* `task.md` that treats the section as its source for the PR. So the agent went hunting by hand and concluded "preprocessing created nothing this cycle" — which was wrong; #81 had merged 1 second before the issue was filed.

## Was it needed?

No. The agent ran ~6 minutes, opened nothing, committed nothing, and closed as a no-op. And it isn't a one-off: #80 (08-05) is the same shape — converge landed, agent dispatched, agent verified everything green and closed. Baselining dispatched an agent on 07-29, 07-30, 07-31, 08-01, 08-02, 08-03, 08-05, 08-06 — essentially every night a converge changed something, against a design whose stated intent is "most nights are agentless and quiet."

## Could it have been prevented?

The forced *run*: it was the right call and shouldn't have been prevented — it pulled a canon head the nightly had missed.

The *agent stage*: yes, and that's precisely the gate's job. Three things stand between here and it not recurring:

1. **The escalation reason is now loggable but still not carried.** #81 makes the worker's stdout appear in the Actions log, so the next escalation will say which branch fired. It still isn't written into the request file, so the dispatch issue can't tell the agent *why* it was woken — the agent re-derives it, which is exactly what produced the wasted no-op here.
2. **A runner-only check failure needs the real output, not a boolean.** `checkTheWorldPasses`/`selfTestPasses` collapse to true/false and swallow findings (`catch { return false }`). Given the checks pass on the identical tree everywhere I can run them, whatever failed in the runner is being thrown away by design.
3. **Version skew across the two stages is structural.** A converge that upgrades its own contract runs the *old* worker and hands off to an agent reading the *new* instructions. That mismatch broke the delivered-artifact handoff on this exact run.

> ⚠️ Nothing here is fixed — this was a read-only investigation. The concrete open items, if you want them filed as issues: (1) carry the escalation reason in the agent-request payload into the dispatch issue; (2) capture check/self-test output instead of collapsing to a boolean; (3) decide whether the worker's own stage should re-read its contract after vendoring, or explicitly tolerate one cycle of skew.

# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the

# edfringe-allocator — this project's own rules

The working knowledge of the EdFringe Allocator pipeline: what may touch the network,
what a year folder owes the solver, and the one datetime invariant everything downstream
assumes. Three of these are checks (`edfringe/offline-stage-imports`,
`edfringe/year-folder-contract`, `edfringe/no-credentialed-path`).

## Datetimes are naive Europe/London, everywhere

Every datetime in the data model is a **naive ISO string in Europe/London local time**
(`edfringe/model.py:3`). Conversion happens once, at the fetch boundary:
`edfringe/extract.py` parses the UTC timestamps out of the fetched event and does
`dt.astimezone(LONDON).replace(tzinfo=None)` (`edfringe/extract.py:78-79`). Downstream —
the solver, the verifier, the renderer, the calendar image — compares those strings and
`datetime.fromisoformat` values directly.

So: never let an aware datetime past `extract`. Mixing one in raises `TypeError` on the
first comparison, usually deep inside the solver where the cause is unrecognisable.
`edfringe/planner_ics.py` is the one place timezone names appear again, and only as iCal
`TZID=Europe/London` text on the way out.

## Code is year-agnostic; only `years/<YYYY>/` changes

Starting a new Fringe year is a **new data folder, never a code edit** — see
`years/README.md` and the `start-a-new-fringe-year` skill in this pack. The window and
the travel buffers reach the solver through `cli.py:73-80` →
`edfringe.scheduling.configure()`, so `years/<YYYY>/config.json` is the source of truth.

Known drift to fix rather than copy: `edfringe/scheduling.py:14-18` still carries the
2026 window and gap values as module defaults, and `edfringe/render.py:139` hardcodes
"Edinburgh Fringe 2026" in the schedule heading. Both are overridden or cosmetic today;
neither is a pattern to follow when adding code.

## The favourites input is a CSV export, not scraped HTML

A view-source of the edfringe.com favourites page is the **logged-out empty state** — it
does not contain the favourites (`docs/FINDINGS.md` §2, README "Good to know" #1). The
resolved design reads the URL column out of the user's CSV export
(`years/<YYYY>/favorites.csv` → `edfringe/favorites.py`). Do not re-attempt to fetch or
parse the favourites page; it is a dead end that has already been paid for once.

## Never introduce a credentialed path

Enforced by `edfringe/no-credentialed-path`; what stays here is why the answer is never
"add the credential". An earlier `cookies.json` held live `auth_token`/`access_token`
for `.edfringe.com` and was committed (`docs/FINDINGS.md` §5) — and it bought nothing,
because show pages are public. The two steps that genuinely need a login (exporting the
favourites CSV, and buying tickets) run in the owner's own browser
(`docs/CLAUDE_FOR_BROWSER.md`), so a change that wants a login is a change that has
taken a wrong turn: move that step to the browser rather than hand the repo a secret.
The retired `old/` prototype still carries the playwright cookie-jar login it was
replaced for — kept for reference, never a pattern to copy.

## `shows_raw/` is the durable source; re-fetching is opt-in

`years/<YYYY>/shows_raw/<slug>.json` is committed and is the source everything else
re-derives from (`edfringe/extract.py` reads it offline). A normal run of the `Fetch show
data` Action re-downloads **nothing** — only the `refresh` input pulls fresh availability
(`.github/workflows/fetch.yml`). Fetching is the one networked stage, so it runs in CI;
extract / travel / schedule / verify / image all run offline from what is committed.

# Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing)

Each pack states what it owns and what it does not. When a rule, doc, skill or check could live in more than one, this table decides it — and "no pack fits" means a new pack or the project's own `local_packs/`, never the baseline by default.

| Pack | Belongs | Does not belong |
|---|---|---|
| `barriers` | directed folder-access graph rules — which directories may never reference which, plus the exceptions each rule allows | where a file should live or naming conventions — that is basics file-placement, not an access barrier |
| `basics` | cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills | technology-specific content — its own tech pack; GitHub Actions workflow or platform behaviour — github-actions; git procedure — git-github |
| `git-github` | git and GitHub procedure: commit layering, branch and merge mechanics, squash-merge recovery, PR and merge-to-main commands | the issue-branch-PR lifecycle rules themselves — basics; workflow YAML and Actions runtime behaviour — github-actions |
| `github-actions` | workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls | git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack |
| `grow_with_claudinite` | rules and tasks for capturing lessons into local packs — extraction, dedup, conversation logs, skill-usage folding | repo housekeeping of issues, PRs and branches — that is tidy-repo; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `tidy-repo` | housekeeping of open issues, pull requests and branches in one repo — triage verdicts, standing trackers, assess-vs-act policy | extracting lessons into packs — that is grow_with_claudinite; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `edfringe-allocator` (local) | the allocator pipeline — its offline/network stage split, per-year data contract, naive-Europe/London datetime invariant | portable practice and general repo hygiene — those live in the vendored Claudinite canon |

input.title: baselining: the escalation reason never reaches the agent — a woken agent has to re-derive why it was woken
input.body:
The baselining worker decides whether an agent is needed, then throws that decision's *reason* away. The agent it wakes has to reconstruct it from the repo, and when it reconstructs it differently the run is wasted.

## What happens

`shouldRequestAgent` (`packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs:165`) has four branches — pending agentic note, withheld workflow file, failed self-test, changed-and-not-green. The worker knows which one fired; it even logs it (`worker.mjs:815-819`, `why`). But the request file it writes carries only the artifacts:

```js
writeFileSync(requestFile, `${JSON.stringify({ marker: AGENT_REQUEST_MARKER, delivered })}\n`);  // worker.mjs:812
```

`readAgentRequest` (`engine/scheduler/preprocess.mjs:88`) reads it, `run.mjs:621` keeps `.delivered` and drops the rest, and `dispatchBody` (`engine/scheduler/dispatch.mjs:96`) renders Context + Delivered. Nothing in the dispatch issue says *why the agent is there*, so `task.md` sends it to re-derive all four conditions from scratch.

## Observed cost

On missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator#82 (scheduler run 31092180798, 2026-08-06): worker converged 11 files, delivered and merged its PR, requested the agent. The agent re-checked all four conditions, found nothing, closed as a no-op — about 6 minutes for zero change. Same shape on that repo's #80 (2026-08-05), and baselining dispatched an agent on 07-29, 07-30, 07-31, 08-01, 08-02, 08-03, 08-05 and 08-06 — essentially every night a converge landed, against a design whose stated intent is that most nights are agentless.

Re-derivation is also not reliably faithful: on #82 the agent concluded "preprocessing created nothing this cycle" while preprocessing had merged its PR one second before the issue was filed.

## Direction

Carry the reason alongside `delivered` — the same named §3 exception that lets `delivered` cross the code→agent boundary, and the same kind of payload (which condition fired, not findings and not instructions). Render it in the dispatch body next to `### Delivered by preprocessing`, so a woken agent starts from "you are here because X" instead of a four-way re-derivation.

Worth deciding at the same time whether §2/§3 of `task.md` should then become *conditional* on the stated reason rather than a fixed sweep — that is where the wasted minutes actually go.

input.title: baselining: checkTheWorldPasses / selfTestPasses discard the very output that would explain the escalation
input.body:
Both gates the baselining worker escalates on collapse a full check run to a boolean and swallow its output:

```js
function checkTheWorldPasses(root) {                      // worker.mjs:268
  ...
  try { node([cw], { CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR: root }); return true; }
  catch { return false; }
}

function selfTestPasses(root) {                           // worker.mjs:410
  ...
  try { node([st, '--strict'], { CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR: root }); return true; }
  catch { return false; }
}
```

`node()` (`worker.mjs:218`) already pipes stdout/stderr, so `execFileSync`'s thrown error carries the findings — and the bare `catch` drops them. The findings are the only thing that says *what* was wrong, and they are the input the woken agent needs most.

The failure mode is worse than "less convenient": these two branches are indistinguishable after the fact. `catch { return false }` cannot tell a genuine finding from the check crashing, timing out, or failing for a runner-environment reason that has nothing to do with the repo's content — and all four produce an identical escalation.

## Evidence this is not hypothetical

missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator#82 (scheduler run 31092180798). By elimination the escalation came from one of these two gates: the delivered stamp was not held back, so no agentic note was pending, and `withheldCount` did not exist in the vendored worker that ran. But on the exact tree that run committed (`64df550`), `check_the_world.mjs` exits 0 across 33 rules and `selftest.mjs --strict` passes — in a working dir and in a `--depth=1` shallow clone matching the runner's checkout. So the run escalated on a check that passes everywhere it can be re-run, and there is no record of what it saw.

(The Actions log doesn't help for that specific run — the pre-#81 `runPreprocessing` buffered the worker's stdout and discarded it on success. The live echo has since landed, so the *log* is now available; the check's own findings still are not, because they never leave the `catch`.)

## Direction

Return the outcome, not a bit: `{ ok, output }` from both helpers, log the findings when non-green, and put a short form of them into the escalation reason (see the companion issue on carrying that reason to the agent). Separately worth distinguishing "check reported findings" from "check could not run" — the first is a judgment case for the agent, the second is closer to a `needs-human`.

---

input.title: A converge that changes the scheduler contract runs the OLD code and hands off to the NEW instructions
input.body:
Baselining's two stages read the mount at different moments, and a converge that changes the contract between them lands astride the change:

- **preprocessing** is the vendored `worker.mjs` the run started with — it converges the mount underneath itself, but the process executing is the *old* code for its whole lifetime;
- **the agent** is dispatched afterwards and reads `task.md` from the *new* mount (its own fresh clone, after the maintenance PR merged).

So on any cycle that changes the handoff, an old producer is paired with a new consumer. `migrations/registry.mjs:96` already names this hazard for one case ("the vendor step earlier in the same cycle replaces the on-disk worker with the new one while the old code is still executing") and works around it with an env handshake. It is not a one-record problem.

## Observed

missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator#82, 2026-08-06. That cycle's converge (canon `076c029` → member commit `64df550`) introduced `deliveredLines` / the `### Delivered by preprocessing` section (`engine/scheduler/dispatch.mjs:84`), the `delivered` payload (`preprocess.mjs:88`, `run.mjs:621`), and the matching §1/§2b of `task.md`.

Result: the run executed the pre-change `dispatch.mjs`, so the dispatch issue carried **no** `### Delivered` section — while the agent read the post-change `task.md`, whose §1 treats that section as its source for the cycle's PR and branch. The agent looked, found nothing, and reported "preprocessing created nothing this cycle". Preprocessing had in fact opened and merged PR #81 one second before the issue was filed.

Benign here (the run was a no-op anyway). It would not be benign on a cycle with real residual work: §2b's "the file must land this cycle, it is not deferrable" depends on the agent locating the branch preprocessing pushed.

## Direction — a decision, not obviously a fix

Three options, and I don't think it's clear which is right:

1. **Re-exec the worker after vendoring** — converge, then hand off to the newly-vendored `worker.mjs` for the delivery half. Removes the skew at its source; costs a re-entrancy contract the worker doesn't have today.
2. **Version the handoff explicitly** — the request payload states which contract it speaks, and `task.md` degrades honestly when the section it expects is absent, instead of reading absence as "nothing was created". Cheapest, and it makes absence unambiguous (today `deliveredLines` documents absence as meaningful — that only holds if the producer could have written it).
3. **Accept one cycle of skew as the rule** and require handoff changes to be introduced in a backward-compatible pair of cycles, the way the env handshake already does for the workflow case. Costs nothing structurally; costs discipline forever.

Whichever is chosen, `consumer-safe-changes.md` looks like the place it should be written down — "a change to the preprocessing→agent handoff is a two-cycle change" is exactly that document's shape.

---

        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level
        # (`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs` and so on), so a test at an unlisted depth
        # was silently never run — which is exactly how vendoring/'s two files sat outside
        # CI. `**` removes depth from the question; what remains is the root list, and
        # engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the moment a tracked test lands

        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)

input.title: baselining: carry the escalation reason to the agent, and stop discarding what the gates said
input.body:
Closes #664, closes #665. Both are the same wasted run seen from two ends, so they land together.

## The problem

The worker decided whether an agent was needed, then threw the decision's *reason* away. The agent it woke re-derived all four conditions from the repo — and on missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator#82 re-derived them wrong, reporting "preprocessing created nothing this cycle" about a cycle that had merged its PR one second earlier, then closing a six-minute run as a no-op.

Both gates it escalates on made that unexplainable after the fact. `catch { return false }` collapsed four different events — findings, a crash, a signal kill, a script that isn't vendored — into one bit, and dropped the findings already sitting in the thrown error's `.stdout`. On #82 the run escalated on a check that passes everywhere it can be re-run, and there is no record of what it saw.

## What changed

**`escalation()` is now the single source for the decision** (`worker.mjs`). It returns `{ code, detail }` or `null`; `shouldRequestAgent()` derives from it instead of repeating a four-branch precedence that could drift out of agreement with it. A test asserts the two never disagree.

**`gateOutcome()` / `GATE_ABSENT` replace the two boolean gates.** A non-zero exit is a verdict about the repo's content; a null status — signal kill, spawn failure — means no verdict was produced at all. Both still escalate (a gate that cannot answer is not permission to proceed), but they are no longer the same sentence, and the full output now reaches the Action log.

**The reason rides the request payload into the dispatch issue** as `### Why the agent is here`:

```
### Why the agent is here
The condition preprocessing escalated on. Start here; the findings themselves are in the repo, not this issue.

- check_the_world reported findings on the converged tree that the deterministic pass could not fix (`checks-not-green`)
```

The condition and its counts, **never the findings** — those stay in the repo for the agent to re-run. That keeps the DESIGN §3 boundary intact: the named exception grows from identity to identity-plus-condition, not to content.

**`task.md` gains §0**, mapping each code to the section that owns it. The named condition is done first and in full; the others stay verifications rather than a fresh hunt, since escalation reports only the *first* condition that fired and a notes night can still carry a withheld workflow file.

## Version skew

Absence stays meaningful throughout. An older vendored worker names no reason, the issue then asserts nothing about why the agent is there, and §0 falls back to the full sweep. So the two stages can be a cycle apart without either one lying — which is the failure #666 describes and this PR does not otherwise address.

## Incidental

The old summary line called a failed self-test "conformance not green". Fixed by construction — there is now one place that names the condition.

## Verification

- Full CI test set: 1183 passing (was 1183 before, +14 new).
- New tests fail against the pre-change code (confirmed by stashing the source and re-running).
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking, 9 advisory — all pre-existing `file-placement` advisories, none on changed lines.
- `node engine/selftest.mjs --strict`: passing.
- Worker → payload → dispatch body exercised end to end; the body above is that run's real output.

content.text:
Understood — no self check-in scheduled. CI events will still wake me if anything fails.

**Both issues are fixed in [PR #667](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/667)** (branch `claude/baselining-escalation-reason-h4ufsh`), landed as one change because they're the same wasted run seen from two ends.

**#665 — the gates:** `checkTheWorldPasses`/`selfTestPasses` are replaced by `runCheckTheWorld`/`runSelfTest` returning `gateOutcome()` — `{ ok, ran, crashed, status, output }`. A non-zero exit is a verdict about the repo; a null status (signal kill, spawn failure) is *no* verdict, and the two are no longer the same sentence. Both still escalate — a gate that can't answer isn't permission to proceed — and the findings that were sitting in the thrown error's `.stdout` now reach the Action log in full.

**#664 — the reason:** `escalation()` returns `{ code, detail }` or `null` and is the single source for the decision; `shouldRequestAgent()` derives from it, with a test asserting they can't drift apart. The reason rides the request payload into the dispatch issue as a `### Why the agent is here` section, and `task.md` gains a §0 mapping each code to the section that owns it.

Two judgment calls worth flagging:

- **The issue said "put a short form of the findings into the reason" — I didn't.** DESIGN §3's exception is identity, not content, and pasting check output through the request file would cross it. The section carries the condition and its counts; the findings stay in the repo for the agent to re-run. Full output goes to the log, which nothing reads programmatically.
- **§2/§2b/§3 did not become conditional.** Escalation reports only the *first* condition that fired, so a notes night can still carry a withheld workflow file — skipping the unnamed sections would drop real work. They're now framed as verifications rather than a fresh hunt, which is where the wasted minutes actually were.

Also fixed incidentally: the old summary line reported a failed self-test as "conformance not green".

Verification: full CI test set 1183 passing (+14 new), new tests confirmed failing against the pre-change source, `check_the_world` 0 blocking (9 pre-existing advisories, none on changed lines), `selftest --strict` green, and the worker→payload→issue-body path exercised end to end.

> ⚠️ Still open: CI on #667 is in progress — I'll be woken on failure and will drive it to green. #666 (the version-skew decision) remains open by design; this PR only makes the new keys degrade honestly when an older worker writes them.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

carry the escalation reason to the agent, and stop discarding what the gates said

Closes #664, closes #665.

The worker decided whether an agent was needed, then threw the decision's reason
away. The agent it woke re-derived all four conditions from the repo — and on
EdFringeAllocator#82 re-derived them wrong, reporting "preprocessing created
nothing this cycle" about a cycle that had merged its PR one second earlier, then
closing a six-minute run as a no-op.

Both gates it escalates on made that unexplainable after the fact. `catch { return
false }` collapsed four different events — findings, a crash, a signal kill, a
script that isn't vendored — into one bit, and dropped the findings that were
already sitting in the thrown error's `.stdout`.

- `escalation()` returns `{ code, detail }` or null and is now the single source
  for the decision; `shouldRequestAgent()` derives from it rather than repeating a
  four-branch precedence that could drift out of agreement with it.
- `gateOutcome()` / `GATE_ABSENT` replace the two boolean gates. A non-zero exit is
  a verdict about the repo; a null status is no verdict at all, and the two are no
  longer the same sentence. Both still escalate — a gate that cannot answer is not
  permission to proceed — and the full output now reaches the Action log.
- The reason rides the request payload into the dispatch issue as `### Why the
  agent is here`: the condition and its counts, never the findings, which stay in
  the repo for the agent to re-run (DESIGN §3).
- task.md gains §0, mapping each code to the section that owns it. The named
  condition is done first and in full; the others stay verifications, since
  escalation reports only the first condition that fired.

Absence stays meaningful throughout: an older vendored worker names no reason, the
issue then asserts nothing about why the agent is there, and §0 falls back to the
full sweep — so the two stages can be a cycle apart without either lying.

Also fixes a reporting bug in the old summary line, which called a failed self-test
"conformance not green".

carry the escalation reason to the agent, and stop discarding what the gates said

Closes #664, closes #665.

The worker decided whether an agent was needed, then threw the decision's reason
away. The agent it woke re-derived all four conditions from the repo — and on
EdFringeAllocator#82 re-derived them wrong, reporting "preprocessing created
nothing this cycle" about a cycle that had merged its PR one second earlier, then
closing a six-minute run as a no-op.

Both gates it escalates on made that unexplainable after the fact. `catch { return
false }` collapsed four different events — findings, a crash, a signal kill, a
script that isn't vendored — into one bit, and dropped the findings that were
already sitting in the thrown error's `.stdout`.

- `escalation()` returns `{ code, detail }` or null and is now the single source
  for the decision; `shouldRequestAgent()` derives from it rather than repeating a
  four-branch precedence that could drift out of agreement with it.
- `gateOutcome()` / `GATE_ABSENT` replace the two boolean gates. A non-zero exit is
  a verdict about the repo; a null status is no verdict at all, and the two are no
  longer the same sentence. Both still escalate — a gate that cannot answer is not
  permission to proceed — and the full output now reaches the Action log.
- The reason rides the request payload into the dispatch issue as `### Why the
  agent is here`: the condition and its counts, never the findings, which stay in
  the repo for the agent to re-run (DESIGN §3).
- task.md gains §0, mapping each code to the section that owns it. The named
  condition is done first and in full; the others stay verifications, since
  escalation reports only the first condition that fired.

Absence stays meaningful throughout: an older vendored worker names no reason, the
issue then asserts nothing about why the agent is there, and §0 falls back to the
full sweep — so the two stages can be a cycle apart without either lying.

Also fixes a reporting bug in the old summary line, which called a failed self-test
"conformance not green".
